Dead Bits is some kinda test-game or something.
It's like "I've put together all these ideas I had jumping around in my head, I'll leave you to fuss over the details."
Gee, thanks. 

Each of the 9 stages has a gimmick. The first one consists entirely of shooting a few block-zombies. The second stage features more block-zombies, and an additional gun. The stage after that? More block-zombies, and a bat. There's a stage where you don't get any weapons, and giant block-golems(?) take pot-shots at you with boulders. These aren't particularly interesting, well-balanced, or even fun gimmicks. They're more like those parts in your favorite games you always dread, but with slippery controls, worse platforming, and cheap deaths. 

Normally I'd write up a long list of ideas that could be implemented, for Dead Bits to approach some level of entertainment. However, I'm going to guess we're far beyond that point now. In fact, with this game I wouldn't even know where to start. Should I write that Dead Bits would be fantastic if it....was never made in the first place? That's not exactly constructive is it? Maybe I could say that it'd be great if this game was really unstable and crashed all the time, so then I wouldn't be able to play it. Hmm...I guess I better quit while I'm behind.

Dead Bits is a game that has the opportunity to be so much more than it is but it falls short to being an actual good game in many ways.

First off is gameplay. The gameplay in this game, while inherently fun, is incredibly basic and mind numbing. You shoot things. That’s it. While that concept is fun in other games, all you do in Dead Bits is hold down mouse one, put your cursor over the enemies, and shoot with infinite ammo while walking backwards. None of the enemies have any major difference besides how spongey they are so it’s basically just fighting the same enemies over and over again.

Next is level design. There isn’t very much thought put into the level design, you just go from point A to point B while shooting things, there is nothing else. The levels are very simplistic and boring, and seven out of nine of the levels are basically clones of each other with different colours and arrangements. Most of the levels are also floating in the air so as you fight things there is a significant possibility of you falling to your death.

Most of the fighting in the game is you just kiting and shooting all of the mobs. When you are shooting you can’t see where you are going and will most likely fall off the map. When you stop shooting to turn around to see where you are going, you will most likely be hit by the enemies that were coming towards you. In the event you die, you must wait the ten or so seconds it takes for your death and resurrection animation to play, and then do the entire level again because there are no check points except in the final level.

There are several instant kill zones in the last few levels which are incredibly annoying the first time you deal with them. You have no idea what they are and some look like something you would pick up. When you die to the instant kill zone you have to redo the entire level again.

There is a major focus on the jumping/platforming aspect of the game but it is very poorly implemented. First comes from the level design. The platforms themselves are either very basic and there is no thought put into it whatsoever or the platforms are annoying with how you have to jump that results with constantly jumping against a wall and sometimes getting up the slope or hitting a bug in the terrain and launching yourself several meters forward and falling to your death.

The mechanics for jumping are also poor. As you jump your character’s movement slows down, so it feels very messy to not only make a single jump but to also continuously jump across multiple platforms. It is also difficult to jump to moving platforms, and farway platforms in general, as there is no real way to tell where you are jumping other than the direction you are facing.

Audio in this game is incredibly loud. Even when playing with my computer’s audio setting incredibly low, the dubstep music that is constantly playing blares through my ears. There are no in game settings to change audio, or settings to change anything other than resolution and basic graphics quality.

I feel like if more effort and care were to be put into a second game, Dead Bits 2 would be a very well made game. The above causes Dead Bits itself is very poorly crafted with many bugs and faulty game design.

It's a pretty okay FPS game. It's not top-notch, however. Here is my review:

     It's a fun and colorful first-person shooter that seems very suiting for a child, yet fun enough for a gamer such as myself to give it a shot. It has 9 unique levels with a cubic pixel art-esque design to it, full of zombies and demons and blocks (Oh, my!), which is great. It has a nice variety of three, count 'em, THREE weapons (as far as I know). It's very simple to start playing and very hard to stop until you beat it.
     It also has a pretty good framerate on my 2003 Windows XP Hewlett-Packard laptop. If you like FPS games but don't have a lot of money or an insane gaming build, then consider buying this. The graphics are still great.

Now, the not-so-good part: 
- The game is extremely short, not even an hour's worth of gameplay
- Level design needs serious work, as there's tons of holes in the ground
- If you're on a moving platform, Quilly (Protagonist) won't move with it, so be very careful.
- Enemies on early levels are poorly placed, seemingly spammed onto the map.
- Very repetitive gameplay
- Imperfect parkour
- Unbalanced weapon to enemy health ratio

Now the part what everyone wants to here. Is it recommended? YES and NO. But personally, I'm leaning more toward YES. The game may not be perfect, but the $1 price tag is fair enough in my opinion. And it goes on sale A LOT. The gameplay is fun nonetheless, and is challenging in certain levels (LEVEL 3, 6 AND 7). Simple controls and very great optimization so even your toaster can run the game at a solid 60 frames per second. It has parkour, kinda, which is difficult which adds to the fun of the challenge (Lv6) and the graphics are good enough for you to make out what it going on. 

    I rate 7/10.

Note to developer(s): I enjoyed your game thoroughly, however the one thing that got me the most was the weapon inbalance and/or the enemies' health. The machine gun only did 20 HP damage, which was very poor when it came to the enemies' health. It does somewhat remind me of Call of Duty Zombies, at around Round 12. The game clearly needs work, but you've done good so far. Keep it up ;)

It's not a horrible game, but finding it on Steam and it's retail price, that's asking for too much.

This game would have been a good few minute time killer to avoid finger tapping, but it wasn't much more than that. I'd expect to see a game such as this on Newgrounds or any other flash game site, maybe even facebook. I'll begin with a general pro/con list then detail the good and bad to each test.

Pros:
+I bought it for $0.14 while it was on the Steam sale
+It did manage to create at least two "startling" scenarios, simply because of enemies appearing in close range with no prior warning, jump-scare if you will
+Some levels kept a focus between platforming and shooting
+The weapons each have unique functions: machine gun, shotgun, melee, explosive
+Weapons are introduced individually to give you a feel for their function
+The levels are generated exactly the same every time, so you'll know exactly where everything is/spawns if you should die or replay the level.

Cons:
-Retail price is 5 dollars
-At any point if there is a possible advantage of terrain or shortcut, the game finds a way of nullifying that with either flying AI or invisible walls that you may see too late
-There is a "bloom" in the crosshair, but any movement, continuous fire, or jumping does nothing to affect your accuracy. Your accuracy is always 100% no matter the condition.
-Crouching does nothing to help you, with 100% accuracy, fast moving enemies, and projectiles mostly in hip range, crouching doesn't provide any advantage.
-Enemies shatter into blocks. Anything too large of a block of that enemy will usually physically impede your movements when you collide with it. This becomes irritating when strafing suddenly comes to a stop because the block is on the ground nearby.
-Any moving platform does not physically move you. This would be fine if all the rotating platforms were all either irregular shaped or squares. This leads to the point where if you're too close to the edge, the second the blocks under your feet become space, you fall, typically to your death.
-Death starts the entire level over, and in most cases having prior knowledge of what's upcoming does nothing to help you progress faster simply because of the grind to kill enemies.
-The enemy AI pathing is both good and bad. It can follow the blocks presented to make a path to you, but sometimes it ignores "space" and walks over the air to reach you. They also may find themselves hung up on walls. And I mean literally as well, sideways on the wall stuck.
-Jumping has a commited jump arc. If anyone remembers the NES games of Castlevania, it's like that. It is exactly like that, buy a wedding ring for that jump because you're stuck with your jump direction til death do you part.
-The game does a terrible job of explaining your environment and how it interacts with you. Several instances will lead to your death. You'll find yourself doing a trail and error with the game's environment if you see something you haven't seen before.
-The levels are exactly the same down to enemy generation, it provides no replayability.
-The game fails to follow a flow, each level is drastically different in what you just played. The only thing that follows, if it does, is just reskinned enemies.
-The slow-motion does not follow your mouse movement and just interferes with your game. If you spin the mouse to fast, your character will turn back and forth between opposite directions because the mouse speed forced in slow-mo can't follow your mouse position. Red Dead Redemption and Max Payne had a function for using slow-mo as an advantage. One Finger Death Punch added slow-mo for flair, but it gave you a break and prevented interfering with the game by not allowing enemies to be within reach during tha time. Dead Bits scripted slow-mo on certain enemies or cues, whether you like it or not.
-Dubstep. It would be fine if the creator of the dubstep didn't also thin himself out to make everything else in the game.
-Music is not consistent throughout the game. You'll play in complete silence sometimes then the music kicks on "cues". Then at other points the music just leaves entirely if playing for too long on one segment.
-There is no pausing the game, you just open the menu and the game continues.
